lesson.title: 802 and All That: How Engineers Standardize the Hardware Underneath
lesson.summary: IEEE standards, produced by the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers through its numbered 802 family, define the physical and link-layer hardware rules, like Ethernet and Wi-Fi, that internet protocols ultimately run on top of.
lesson.body:
The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, almost always shortened to IEEE, is a professional association that, among many other activities, publishes formal technical standards through its IEEE Standards Association. Where the RFC series from the last chapter documents internet protocols specifically, IEEE's scope is much broader, covering an enormous range of electrical and electronic engineering. For networking, the part that matters most is a family of standards known as IEEE 802, which governs the local area network hardware and low-level protocols that sit underneath the internet protocols most people are familiar with.

The 802 project takes its name from when it started, February 1980, and it is organized into working groups, each numbered and each responsible for one specific technology. IEEE 802.3 defines Ethernet, the wired local area networking standard used in offices, homes, and data centers. IEEE 802.11 defines Wi-Fi, the wireless equivalent. IEEE 802.1 covers higher level concerns that apply across multiple 802 technologies, including 802.1Q, which defines how switches tag traffic with VLAN identifiers so that one physical network can be logically split into several isolated ones. Each of these is its own standalone document, but together they form a coherent family covering how devices on a shared local link actually talk to each other.

Ethernet's history shows how a standard turns a useful invention into something universal. It began as an experimental system at Xerox PARC in the 1970s, and after Digital Equipment Corporation, Intel, and Xerox worked out a joint specification, IEEE formalized it as 802.3 in 1983. Once the electrical signaling, cabling rules, and frame format were nailed down in a public document, any manufacturer could build a network card that correctly interoperated with any other manufacturer's card and any other manufacturer's switch. That is also why a modern laptop's gigabit Ethernet port and a network card from the early 1990s still share the same fundamental frame format: the standard was designed to be extended with faster speeds over time rather than replaced outright, and 802.11 has followed a similar pattern, with amendments like 802.11ac and 802.11ax adding capability to the same base standard rather than starting over.

IEEE standards are a de jure standard in the sense introduced earlier, formally adopted and versioned by a recognized body, but the norms around them differ from the RFC series in a telling way. For much of their history, IEEE standards documents had to be purchased, unlike RFCs, which have always been free, though IEEE has since made some widely used documents, including 802.3 and 802.11, freely available through its Get IEEE 802 program. Different standards bodies really do operate under different rules, and it is worth noticing when a specification costs money and when it does not.

The reason this chapter matters for everything that follows is architectural. IEEE 802 standards define how bits move across one physical link and how devices on that link address each other, which is the foundation the internet's higher layers are built on top of. An IP packet, which later chapters cover in detail, does not travel across a network by itself. It is carried inside an Ethernet or Wi-Fi frame for each physical hop of its journey, and that frame's exact format is exactly what IEEE 802.3 and 802.11 specify.
